# PART I — PACS: full observed results and findings


**Verdict: negative. The coupling route is closed, and the reason generalises.**
Everything below is measured on t2015 only. No t2017 was used anywhere in this work.

---

## 1. The hypothesis and why it was worth testing

§C.18 is the sharpest structural finding in the project:

| MASC accuracy measured on | value |
|---|---|
| all gold spans (`a_gold`) | **81.20** |
| spans MATE actually extracts (`a_selected`) | **80.52** |
| spans MATE **misses** | **86.73** |

The extractor systematically selects the spans its own classifier is **worst** at. The
anti-correlation is `a_selected − a_gold = −0.68`. MADSC's published numbers imply the
opposite sign (`a` 84.18 against 82.34 gold-span, i.e. **+1.84**) — a ~2.5-point swing in
`a`, almost exactly our joint gap.

The cause is structural and self-inflicted: Chapters C/D deliberately built MATE and MASC as
*decorrelated* model families, which is ideal for ensembling and exactly wrong for joint
MABSA.

**Why this reframed the target.** The bar had been read as "get `a` to 83.1 on all gold
spans", which is above every published number. But spans at **86.73** accuracy already exist
in this system — they are simply not selected. Holding MATE@τ at 87.8, moving `a_selected`
from 80.4 to ~83.5 clears 72.9. That is a selection problem inside a population we already
have, not a demand for SOTA polarity.

---

## 2. The arithmetic — including a threshold error worth recording

Micro-F1 is `2·TP/(|pred| + |gold|)`. Dropping a prediction whose probability of being
correct is `q` therefore improves F1 exactly when

```
q < F1/2          (derivation: 2(TP−q)/(K−1+G) > 2TP/(K+G)  ⇔  q < TP/(K+G) = F1/2)
```

which is **0.353** at our operating point (TP 728, kept 1032, gold 1037, F1 70.6).

**Both I and the ChatGPT proposal initially used `q > 0.5`.** That rule minimises *expected
error count* (`2(1−q)` if extracted vs `1` if skipped) — a different objective — and it
over-drops. With **oracle** knowledge of `q`:

| cut | predictions dropped | TP lost | projected F1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **q < 0.353** (correct for F1) | 187 | 25.2 | **74.68** |
| q < 0.40 | 205 | 32.1 | 74.66 |
| q < 0.50 (the intuitive rule) | 253 | 53.6 | 74.28 |

**74.68 clears the 72.9 bar.** Everything that follows is about whether `q` is obtainable
without the answers.

---

## 3. The determinability signal `q`, and its validation

`q` = probability that a candidate's polarity will be predicted correctly, estimated from
four architecturally distinct out-of-fold towers (`oof_btwL`, `oof_btw`, `oof_deb`,
`oof_twrob`).

**Estimator choice, measured not assumed.** Vote-counting (`k/4`) throws away most of the
signal — within the k=2 bucket the true `q` spans 0.29–0.71:

| k of 4 towers correct | n | `q` range | mean `q` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 356 | 0.00–0.35 | 0.055 |
| 1 | 278 | 0.13–0.50 | 0.297 |
| 2 | 303 | 0.29–0.71 | 0.508 |
| 3 | 462 | 0.43–0.86 | 0.717 |
| 4 | 1780 | 0.68–1.00 | 0.961 |

**Cross-family transfer test.** Estimate `q` from 2 towers, then predict whether the *other*
2 architectures get the same aspect right:

| q from | predicts | AUC (vote count) | AUC (mean softmax) |
|---|---|---|---|
| btwL+btw | deb+twrob | 0.8744 | **0.9217** |
| btwL+deb | btw+twrob | 0.8439 | 0.9022 |
| btwL+twrob | btw+deb | 0.8533 | 0.9028 |
| btw+deb | btwL+twrob | 0.8554 | 0.9049 |
| btw+twrob | btwL+deb | 0.8454 | 0.9023 |
| deb+twrob | btwL+btw | 0.8547 | 0.9046 |
| **mean** | | **0.8545** | **0.9064** |

So per-example polarity difficulty is a largely **model-independent** property of examples —
**not** merely the shared blind spot §D.11 warned about — and the softmax estimator is worth
**+0.05 AUC** over vote-counting. Reference: §D.2 measured MASC max-probability at AUC
**0.659** for the same target.

`q` is saved in `data/qdet_train.npz` (3179 aspects). 779 (24.5%) fall below 0.5; 576
(18.1%) below the correct 0.353 cut.

---

## 4. PACS itself — architecture and results

`experts/pacs.py`. One encoder, two heads:

```
deberta-v3-large ─► word representations hw
                      ├── proj → BIO emissions → linear-chain CRF   (anchor / MATE)
                      └── span pooling [mean, first, last] → MLP    (polarity / MASC)

  U(s) = A(s) · P(ŷ|s)^λ          A(s) = mean(1 − P(O)) over the span
```

Both heads read the **same** `hw`, so a joint loss backprops through both at once — which is
what a post-hoc product over frozen scores structurally cannot do. TARKAN's identity is
preserved: BIO anchor generation with a CRF, aspect-conditioned polarity, student-only
inference.

### Results (seed 42, 16 epochs, identical recipe throughout)

| arm | MATE@τ dev | MATE@τ test | `a_selected` dev | **`a_selected` test** | joint dev | **joint test** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **control** (`lam_joint` 0, `lam_det` 0) | 84.70 | 84.83 | 78.88 | **76.91** | 66.82 | **65.24** |
| **determinability-ranked** (`lam_det` 1.0) | 84.96 | 85.17 | 77.60 | **74.00** | 65.93 | **63.02** |
| Δ | +0.26 | +0.34 | −1.28 | **−2.91** | −0.89 | **−2.22** |

**The result is negative and of the opposite sign to the hypothesis.** Training the extractor
to prefer polarity-determinable spans made its selected spans **harder** for its own
classifier (`a_selected` −2.91) and cost 2.22 joint F1. At −2.22 this is well clear of the
§D.20 ±1.31 single-pair detection floor, so it is a real degradation rather than noise.

Reading: forcing the anchor score to encode difficulty **fights the tagging objective** and
damages both. MATE@τ rose slightly (+0.34) while the polarity of what it selected collapsed.

### A structural limit found while designing the control
Hard parameter sharing costs extraction before PACS even starts: the shared-encoder control
gets MATE@τ **84.83** against the dedicated tagger's **85.77** and the 5-member ensemble's
**87.01**. PACS therefore begins at joint 65.24 and **cannot be a standalone system** — no
coupling gain closes 5+ points to the 70.4 ensemble. Its only plausible use was as a
better-ranked *candidate source*, which §5–6 then tested directly and more cheaply.

---

## 5. Two bugs found before they could fake a result

Both would have produced a *plausible null* attributable to the hypothesis rather than to the
code. Both were caught by printing intermediate quantities, not the final metric.

**(a) Double zero-init dead branch.** The first version had a polarity→emissions feedback
gate with **both** the gate scalar `alpha` and its projection `fb` zero-initialised:

```
∂L/∂alpha = fb    = 0        ∂L/∂fb = alpha = 0
```

Both parameters had **identically zero gradient forever**. The branch was dead code that
looked principled and printed a plausible `alpha +0.000`. It was also applied only to gold
spans during training and **never at inference** — train/test inconsistent. Removed; the
joint margin is the actual coupling.

**(b) Vacuous batch-mean margin.** The hard-negative loss compared batch **means**:

```
lj = relu(margin + Un.mean() − Ug.mean())
```

That is one scalar constraint per batch, which ordinary training already satisfies. The
control arm logs the term even though `lam_joint = 0` there, and it read **0.0013 by epoch 8
and 0.0000 by epoch 12 without ever being optimised.** Running the coupled arm would have
returned "coupling does nothing" as an artifact of the loss. Replaced with a true pairwise
margin — every gold span against **its own** boundary errors,
`relu(m + U_neg − U_gold[owner]).mean()` — verified on a live batch (15 gold spans → 45
negatives, every negative owned by a gold span in the same sentence, spot-checks are genuine
boundary shifts).

**(c) Conceptual, also corrected.** The first formulation treated "0 of 4 towers correct" as
a ground-truth *indeterminability label*, which contradicts §D.11's own finding that residual
errors are **consensus** errors. `q` was made a Laplace-smoothed estimate,
`q̂ = (k+α)/(4+2α)`, and the loss given an absolute threshold rather than a pure ranking —
noting that mapping `d = k/4` to `u = 2q−1` changes **nothing** in a pairwise ranking loss,
since it is a monotone affine transform. The real content of the `q > 0.5` insight is a
threshold, which the pairwise form never had.

---

## 6. Follow-up probes: why PACS failed

### 6a. Predict `q` from the text instead (`experts/qpredict.py`)
Rather than force the extractor to internalise `q`, estimate it in a separate model and apply
it at decision time. Trained on **3635 OOF MATE candidates** (gold span → `q`, non-gold span
→ 0; 815 non-gold, mean target 0.563, 36.2% below the 0.353 cut), 4 epochs, loss 0.686 →
0.465. Consumed by `decide.py --qhat`.

| acceptance score | dev | **test** |
|---|---|---|
| geometric product (standing) | **70.16** | **70.43** |
| q̂ alone (`--qhat-mix 1.0`) | 69.52 | 69.81 |
| q̂ × product (`--qhat-mix 0.5`) | 70.03 | 69.96 |

Below baseline. The reason is directly measurable:

| score | AUC for "this (span, polarity) pair is correct" |
|---|---|
| **oracle `q`** — other classifiers **+ gold labels** | **0.906** |
| geometric product (standing) | 0.7334 |
| **learned q̂ from the text** | **0.7049** |
| span evidence S | 0.6938 |
| MASC max probability | 0.6605 |

The learned predictor is **worse than the product it replaces**.

### 6b. Use member disagreement — a feature §D.2 never tested
§D.2's eleven features used the entropy of the **averaged** distribution, never inter-member
disagreement. At test time we do have 19 members' behaviour, so this is the computable proxy
for whatever scores 0.906.

| score | AUC | dev | **test F1** |
|---|---|---|---|
| geometric product | 0.7334 | 70.16 | **70.43** |
| member agreement alone | 0.6502 | — | — |
| member variance | 0.6609 | — | — |
| **product × agreement** | **0.7670** | 70.19 | 69.70 |
| product² × agreement | — | 70.18 | 70.06 |
| product³ × agreement | — | 70.19 | 70.64 |

**+0.034 AUC converts to nothing.** Dev is flat at 70.16–70.19 while test scatters
69.70–70.64, entirely inside the ±1.31 floor. Third independent confirmation of §C.24's
"improving the judge's AUC by +0.02 did not convert into F1".

---

## 7. ★ The mechanism — why the 74.68 oracle is unreachable

| source of `q` | AUC |
|---|---|
| other classifiers **compared to the gold labels** | **0.906** |
| the geometric product | 0.733 |
| a model reading the **text** | 0.705 |
| the same ensemble's **disagreement, without labels** | 0.650 |

**`q` is a property of model competence, not a readable property of the input.** It is
recoverable at 0.906 only by running independent classifiers *and comparing them to the
answer*. Strip the labels and the identical ensemble's disagreement carries 0.650 — barely
above MASC confidence.

So **74.68 was never a target**: the information that would fix the selection exists only
once you already know the answer. This is the deepest statement of the §D.2 ceiling (a
selector fitted directly on test cannot beat the honest one), and it reconciles with §D.11
rather than contradicting it — the residual errors are consensus errors **and** the consensus
cannot identify which of its own answers are the wrong ones.

---

## 8. What this closes, and what it does not

**Closed.** The extraction↔polarity coupling route, by three independent attacks: internalise
`q` in the extractor (−2.22), predict `q` from text (AUC 0.705 < 0.733), estimate it from
member disagreement (+0.034 AUC → 0.0 F1).

**Not overturned.** §C.18 remains a true and interesting observation about the system — the
extractor really does select the spans its classifier handles worst. What PACS establishes is
that the anti-correlation is **not actionable**, because acting on it requires a competence
estimate that only the labels provide.

**Standing result unchanged: 70.32** (choice-free, all correct members equal-weight) /
**70.62** (fixed 19-member structure). 15 of 19 t2015 baselines cleared; SGBIS 71.1,
DQPSA 71.9, VLHA 72.5, MADSC 72.9 remain above.

**Reproduce the arithmetic without a GPU:**
`python3 experts/decide.py --pool pools/final19 --w-grid 0.0` → dev 70.16 / test 70.43.

  What the frozen pool proved (both results reverse Chapter C's own diagnosis):

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │                finding                 │       number       │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │ gold pairs lost to extraction          │ 92                 │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │ gold pairs lost to polarity            │ 186 ← 2.02× larger │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │ recoverable (perfect-selector ceiling) │ 759 → F1 84.52     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

  §C.19 concluded "the route runs through MATE precision, not polarity" and
  eight experiments followed that. Counted directly it's backwards — and NEG
  recall is 57.4, with 158 of the 186 errors being minority↔NEU.

  Selection is closed for a stronger reason than dev noise. A logistic over 11
  decision features fitted directly on the test set scores 70.77 — no better
  than the honest dev fit (70.83), against a ceiling of 84.52. The information
  isn't there to be estimated. Decode-time class bias dies the same way (dev is
  flat across the whole β range while test wanders ±0.5).

  So: a must reach ~83.5, above every published t2015 number (MADSC 82.34).
  Chapter C measured eight rearrangements of ~200M encoders that don't get
  there. Running now is the honest alternative — a QLoRA'd Llama-3.1-8B scored
  on three option tokens, with the training objective being literally the
  inference computation. Chained behind it: re-scoring all 15 encoder members
  onto the union pool (test recall 91.13 → 93.44, from giving PDQ-MATE a third
  role as a candidate source).

  One structural fix landed ahead of the result: a log-average is equal-weight,
  so one strong member among fifteen weak ones gets averaged down to 1/16 of the
  vote. The pool now carries the two groups separately with a single dev-tuned
  mixing scalar.

● Their read matches the measurements, and two of their three D1 evaluation
  modes were already covered — worth being precise about which:

  B (residual, z_base + α(z_D1 − z_base)) is not a separate experiment. It's
  algebraically identical to the log-space group mixing already in
  pool.py/decide.py: (1−w)·log p_base + w·log p_llm is that residual with α = w.
  The w sweep runs it.

  C (selective gating) was genuinely missing — now added. It restricts the LLM's
  correction to rows where the base is undecided at the NEU/minority boundary,
  which is where D.1 put 158 of the 186 errors. Their reasoning for why it
  differs from the failed §C.27 NEU-escape is right and worth stating precisely:
  C.27 amplified a residual trained from the same features exactly where the
  base was most often correct (NEU recall 88.2); this hands the decision to a
  different model class only where the base admits it can't tell. It costs a
  third dev-fitted scalar though, and §C.24(b)/§C.26 both punished extra dev
  degrees of freedom — so it reports alongside the 2-scalar rule rather than
  replacing it. Smoke-tested as a correct no-op.

  A (standalone) comes free from the member's own gold-span accuracy.

  Two corrections to their framing:

  - The PDS pairing they propose already exists — the three pds_res_*_wn0
  members (zero-init residual + signed-margin hinge + w_none=0) are inside the
  base ensemble that D1 gets mixed against. That combination is measured
  automatically, not a new build.
  - Their arithmetic uses 71.37 / a=81.21. The frozen pool says the real
  dev-selected baseline is 70.37 / a=80.26 — §C.26 had already ruled 71.37
  non-selectable, and reproducing core-8 confirms it (dev matches C.23 to 0.01,
  test differs 0.57 purely on τ tie-breaking). So it's 27 flips from a 70.37 
  base, needing a ≈ 83.5, not 83.0. The lever is unchanged; the target is
  slightly harder than they think.

  Training is at step 150/597, ~10.1 s/step. First dev eval in ~8 minutes.

  which direction?                                                              
                                                                                
  That is basically a multimodal intervention signal.                           
                                                                                
  And that fits your PDS idea extremely naturally.

● Built and committed. To answer directly: yes, and one implementation gives 
  both uses.

  experts/masc_qwenvl.py reads data/images/twitter2015/*.jpg directly — no
  caption anywhere in the path:

  - --counterfactual — the teacher performs the intervention itself: Δ = P(y | 
  tweet, aspect, IMAGE) − P(y | tweet, aspect), sign only. This is strictly
  better-founded than the current PDS teacher, which asked Llama to judge 
  subjectively whether an image shifts sentiment and answered "no shift" 75% of
  the time. Keeping only the sign isn't a stylistic choice — §C.27 measured that
  regressing on the teacher's magnitude actively fails, because its scale is a
  bias to resist (mean confidence 0.795 with a 6.8:1 POS skew). Output is
  written in pds_teacher.py's exact format, so the proven §C.27 formulation
  consumes it with zero changes.
  - default — a restricted-token MASC member that sees pixels, the only one in
  the ensemble that will.

  Where I'd push back on their plan: they say "don't use Qwen as a MASC
  classifier, it's been tested and capped at 79–80." The A15 number is 80.76,
  which is higher than every member we have, and A15's pessimistic verdict was
  about Qwen as the entire system — its MATE was 85.14 against our current
  87.01. As a polarity member it only does the job it was already best at, and
  §C.25's lesson is that the ensemble converts decorrelated partners, not merely
  strong ones. A pixel-reading member is maximally decorrelated from 15
  caption-fed encoders.

  Vision tower frozen, LoRA confined to the language tower by regex (the visual
  blocks share projection names), max_pixels capping visual tokens — that's the
  entire memory story on a 16GB T4. It needs a feasibility benchmark before I
  spend hours on it, which I'll run as soon as the GPU frees.

● Recorded. The honest read on where this leaves things:

  The bottleneck has been localised, and it isn't what the campaign has been 
  attacking. It is not member quality (an 8B ties a 355M encoder), not diversity
  (49 uniquely-right aspects, oracle 85.63), and not combiner form (three forms
  tried, all invert). It is that n_dev = 1122 with σ ≈ 1.2 cannot resolve the 
  ~0.5 differences being chased, so every fitted combiner fits noise. That's now
  five independent dev/test inversions, and §C.7 already showed moving the fit
  to OOF train data doesn't rescue it either.

  Two things still matter, and I'm holding to both:

  1. The joint metric isn't gold-span accuracy. Everything above measures argmax
  accuracy on gold spans. In the actual objective the 8B's confidence also
  enters the selection score, and the pool changed (union recall 93.44). It can
  help there while being flat here. decide.py on the union pool is the real test
  — that's what queue26 is for.
  2. Qwen2.5-VL is still the one genuinely new information source. Every finding
  above concerns rearranging signals already in the system. Pixels are not in
  the system.

  I'd also flag a concrete new option I found while checking: NUSTM/VLP-MABSA is
  live on GitHub, and AoM's official checkpoint — already working in graft/ at 
  t2015 68.42 — is itself built on VLP-MABSA's pretraining. So the
  MABSA-specific pretraining Chapter B §7c blamed for the dead visual stream is
  reachable without new pretraining. It needs the legacy env
  (py3.8/torch1.13/transformers3.4), so it's a real cost, and D.6 tempers how
  much another decorrelated member is likely to convert — but it's the one
  member class carrying information no member here has.

  queue26 starts as soon as the 8B finishes scoring the test pool.

● This produced the sharpest finding in Chapter D, and it's a real result even
  though it's negative:

  More teacher signal is not better teacher signal. The pixels genuinely carry
  ~3× the evidence of the caption (76% of aspects vs 25%), and the POS:NEG skew
  collapsed from 6.8:1 to 2.16:1 — which answers §C.25's own objection that the
  old teacher's skew "would teach images make things positive, a bias not a
  mechanism." Both metrics moved the right way. And every member got uniformly
  ~1.1 worse.

  The inversion is the point: the caption teacher's 75% abstention rate looked 
  like its main defect and was partly its main virtue. Abstaining is what kept
  its 25% of direction labels clean. An evidence teacher's value is set by the
  precision of its non-abstentions, not its coverage.

  That's a transferable lesson for the paper, independent of whether the bar
  falls.

  queue30 now tests whether the floor is the whole story (0.20 / 0.35 vs 0.05).
  If a higher floor recovers past 78.50, the mechanism works and was
  mis-thresholded. If it doesn't, the image-teacher route is closed and I'll say
  so.

  Non-monotonic and all ~1 point below the caption teacher. Thresholding is not 
  the problem — the image-teacher route is closed.

  The better explanation, which I should have seen earlier: Δ is the difference 
  of two noisy estimates. Qwen's own polarity judgments are only ~80% accurate,
  so differencing two such distributions gives roughly √2× the noise of either
  arm while the signal being extracted is small. The caption teacher was asked 
  the shift question directly and returned one noisy answer; the counterfactual
  construction is more principled but noisier in practice. Recording:

● This is the decisive answer to their "you only need 27 flips" framing, and it
  closes the axis rigorously:

  Flip precision is a coin toss at every confidence level.

  ┌───────────┬───────┬───────┬───────┬───────────┬─────┐
  │ 8B conf > │ flips │ right │ wrong │ precision │ net │
  ├───────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┼───────────┼─────┤
  │ 0.00      │ 97    │ 45    │ 52    │ 0.464     │ −7  │
  ├───────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┼───────────┼─────┤
  │ 0.70      │ 68    │ 31    │ 37    │ 0.456     │ −6  │
  ├───────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┼───────────┼─────┤
  │ 0.90      │ 35    │ 18    │ 17    │ 0.514     │ +1  │
  ├───────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┼───────────┼─────┤
  │ 0.95      │ 18    │ 8     │ 10    │ 0.444     │ −2  │
  └───────────┴───────┴───────┴───────┴───────────┴─────┘

  Net gain from N flips at precision p is N(2p−1). At p ≈ 0.47 every flip rule
  is net negative, and the single cell above 0.5 (p = 0.514) would need 945 
  flips to net +27 — there are only 97 disagreements in existence. The 27 flips
  are arithmetically sufficient and empirically unreachable.

  The base rates explain it: the 8B fixes 45 of 179 wrong-polarity cases (25.1%)
  but breaks 47 of 728 correct ones (6.5%) — net −2. Let me bound what any

● Committed and pushed. Their suggestion produced the session's most important
  measurement — just not the one they expected.

  The "27 flips" target is arithmetically right and empirically unreachable, and
  now I can say exactly why.

  Net gain from N flips at precision p is N(2p−1). The 8B's flip precision is
  0.46–0.51 at every confidence level — a coin toss. The one cell above 0.5
  would need 945 flips to net +27; only 97 disagreements exist. It fixes 45 of
  179 wrong cases and breaks 47 of 728 correct ones: net −2.

  The reason is the finding I'd been missing all session. Polling all 19 members
  on the 179 wrong cases:

  - 140 have at least one member right (78%)
  - but only 7 have a majority right (3.9%)
  - mean members correct: 17.4/19 on correct cases vs 3.9/19 on wrong ones

  The pool isn't split on its failures — it's confidently wrong together. These
  are consensus errors. Only 7 of 179 are recoverable by any unweighted rule,
  worth +0.62. The other 133 need per-example knowledge of which minority of 1–5
  members happens to be right, which is exactly what D.2 proved unavailable
  from every signal the system produces.

  That makes every negative in Chapters C and D a single corollary: adding a 
  19th voice to a pool that is confidently wrong together changes nothing. §C.7,
  §C.17, §C.21, §C.24, §D.6, §D.8, §D.10 all follow. It also reconciles the two
  ceilings independently — the member-oracle bound is 83.9, matching the 84.5
  perfect-selector bound D.1 found from the opposite direction. The entire 70.4
  → 84 gap is per-example model selection.

  So I'd revise their conclusion in one respect. They wrote "this is where the 
  remaining 2.5 F1 has to come from — new polarity information." That's right,
  but D.11 sharpens what qualifies: new information that is decorrelated from 
  the existing consensus, not merely from individual members. The 8B and Qwen-VL
  were both decorrelated from individual members and both joined the same
  consensus on the hard cases. A backbone with MABSA pretraining is the only
  candidate left that might sit outside it — and it has to enter as a backbone,
  not a member.

  Standing result: 70.43, selection-free, dev-best and test-best.

● Running. To be clear about why this is a real shot and not a repeat:

  I built the counterfactual because differencing is the more principled way to
  isolate an image's effect — and it lost to noise, badly. D.10 concluded that
  asking a weak teacher outright beat differencing it against itself. I wrote
  that sentence and then didn't act on it. This is the missing cell:

  - §C.25 asked the question directly — but Llama only ever saw a BLIP caption
  - §D.9/D.10 used the real pixels — but estimated the shift by differencing

  Nobody has asked the question directly of a model looking at the actual image.
  It's also one forward pass instead of two, so it's cheaper than the thing
  that failed.

  The smoke signature is the encouraging part: 83% abstention with a ~1:1 
  POS:NEG skew. D.9 established both criteria independently — abstention is what
  kept the caption teacher's labels clean, and its 6.8:1 skew was "a bias, not
  a mechanism." The caption teacher was selective but biased; the counterfactual
  was balanced but indiscriminate. This is the first one with both right.

  79.27 — identical recipe, only the teacher's labels differ. ~1h.

  Being honest about the ceiling even if it wins: PDS bought +0.26 last time,
  and D.11 says the residual errors are consensus errors that a training-time
  signal must actually shift, not just add a view to. If this teacher is
  genuinely better, the follow-up that matters is applying it to more than three
  members — moving the consensus rather than decorating it.

✻ Baked for 10m 48s

● Monitor event: "Direct image teacher PDS members and the confound check"

● qdpds_btwL → 76.95, against the caption baseline's 78.50 (−1.55) and even
  below the counterfactual's 77.24. So the direct question doesn't rescue it
  either — both pixel-based teachers lose to the caption teacher.

  That points at a cause I hadn't considered, and it isn't the teacher at all.
  Look at what the student can actually see: masc_pds feeds the residual head
  CLIP pooled visual features. The caption teacher's directions are derivable
  from coarse scene content — exactly what CLIP pooling encodes — because the
  caption was generated from that same coarse content. Qwen's directions come
  from embedded text, facial expression, object condition, image/text contrast:
  real signal, but not representable in a CLIP pooled vector. A teacher that
  sees more than the student can represent produces targets the student cannot
  fit, and unlearnable targets are indistinguishable from noise.

  That would explain D.9, D.10 and D.12 with one mechanism, and it predicts the
  remaining two members land at ~−1.1 to −1.5 as well. Waiting to see whether
  that holds.

  D.9/D.10 were confounded by my bug — retracted

  pds_margin_loss hardcoded w_pos = 0.147, the inverse frequency of the caption
  teacher's 687:101. Its own docstring said so. Every Qwen-VL member inherited
  that constant while its teacher was 1394:644, needing 0.462. Re-run correctly:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬───────┐
  │          bertweet-large          │  w_pos  │ test  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼───────┤

  Two conclusions I recorded are withdrawn:

  - ✗ "More teacher signal is not better teacher signal" — not supported.
  Correctly weighted, the teacher with 3× the evidence performs the same.
  - ✗ "Asking a weak teacher outright beats differencing it against itself" —
  reversed. Differencing ties; asking directly is the weaker one. I built D.12
  on a lesson my own bug manufactured.

  What survives is real but narrower: an auxiliary direction loss must be
  balanced against its own teacher's distribution — inheriting a constant from a
  different teacher silently costs ~1.2 points. D.9/D.10 stay in the ledger
  behind a retraction banner rather than being edited away.

  D.12: the mechanism works and still doesn't convert

  The direct teacher is the most selective (81% no-shift) and the only
  NEG-leaning one — and it transferred exactly as designed: NEG recall 52.2 → 
  59.3 (+7.1), aimed squarely at D.1's worst number, for −0.78 accuracy.

  Ensemble: 69.98 / 70.07 / 70.20 against the standing 70.43.

  That's the cleanest D.11 demonstration yet — a confirmed mechanism, correctly
  aimed at the diagnosed failure, buying +7.1 on our weakest class, and outvoted
  by a consensus that is confidently wrong together.

  Two counterfactual towers are re-running to put the correction on three points
  instead of one. Standing result: 70.43.

● Both mechanisms built, committed, and running as a controlled 4-way comparison
  on bertweet-large (baseline / factorized / CER / both), ~35 min.

  To your constraint: TARKAN's core is untouched. Anchors, teacher-guided
  evidence, KG, KAN, auxiliary ASC, student-only inference — all unchanged. Only
  the polarity head and its auxiliary losses differ. This is an extension, not
  a replacement.

  Why these two and not the other four. CER is the only proposal in that list
  that attacks D.11 head-on. D.11 established the residual errors are consensus
  errors — 3.9/19 members right, only 7 of 179 with majority support — so adding
  voters provably can't help and D.2 showed no selector can pick the right
  minority. CER trains against the shortcut itself. And the precondition checks
  out: the OOF buffer has the same signature as the test failures (0.65/4
  members right vs 3.62/4; 347 of 653 collapsing to NEU; NEG worst at 35.9% of
  its class). That's a faithful proxy, which I verified before writing any
  training code.

  One bug worth flagging, because it nearly produced a false negative. My first
  factorized implementation supervised the two heads but never the composed
  decision. bertweet-base went 59.7 → 56.5 — below the 58.5 majority class —
  against a 73.8 baseline. Had I run that straight on the real tower I'd have
  recorded "factorized polarity fails" and moved on. It was uncalibrated
  composition, not a bad idea: adding an NLL term on the composed log-probs
  recovers it to 73.08. The factorization is a structural prior on the decision,
  not a substitute for supervising it.

  Being honest about expectations: D.11 still says member-level gains don't
  convert. The difference here is that CER changes what the training optimizes
  on exactly the population that defines the ceiling — if it moves those cases,
  the consensus itself shifts rather than acquiring one more dissenting voice.

● Both mechanisms measured, both negative — but CER's failure taught me
  something that changes how I read the whole campaign.

  ┌─────────────────┬───────┬───────┬───────┐
  │     variant     │  dev  │ test  │   Δ   │
  ├─────────────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┤
  │ baseline        │ 77.45 │ 78.69 │ —     │
  ├─────────────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┤
  │ factorized head │ 76.92 │ 77.72 │ −0.97 │
  ├─────────────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┤
  │ CER             │ 69.70 │ 74.35 │ −4.34 │
  ├─────────────────┼───────┼───────┼───────┤
  │ both            │ 72.64 │ 75.89 │ −2.80 │
  └─────────────────┴───────┴───────┴───────┘

  CER's premise is half wrong, and that's the finding. It assumes the consensus
  is wrong because the family learned a shared shortcut — something learnable
  away. But D.11 also measured 39 of 179 test failures where no member of 19 is 
  right, and the training buffer necessarily contains that same population.
  Those are most plausibly annotation noise or genuine ambiguity. Nothing 
  distinguishes "shared shortcut" from "wrong label" from the outside, so
  training hard on the buffer teaches noise — which is exactly what a −4.34
  collapse with dev falling −7.75 looks like.

  So D.11 reads one level deeper than I wrote it: the residual errors aren't 
  merely errors the family shares — a substantial part of them is irreducible.
  That reframes the remaining 2.5 F1 as partly unavailable rather than merely
  hard to reach, and it's consistent with both independent ceilings
  (perfect-selector 84.5, member-oracle 83.9) sitting well below 100 on a pool
  that already contains the right span.

  One process note worth your attention: my first factorized implementation
  supervised the two heads but not the composed decision, and bertweet-base fell
  to 56.5 — below the 58.5 majority class. Had I run that on the strong tower
  I'd have recorded "factorized polarity fails" for entirely the wrong reason.
  It's now fixed and the negative above is real.

  Three weaker CER settings are running (margin-only at 10× weaker, replay-only,
  hardest-failures-only) so the mechanism gets a fair test before I close it.
  ~25 min.

  mislabelled examples, whereas the hinge saturates once the gold logit clears
  the consensus logit by the margin and then stops. It's a bounded correction
  against an unbounded one, on data known to be ~50% noise at high confidence.

  the four. Deberta tower next.

● CER and RER are closed. Committed and pushed.

  I have to walk back my own excitement. The +0.58 I flagged as "the first
  positive in a long while" does not survive its own sweep. Eleven
  configurations scatter ±0.6 around baseline with no monotone structure in any
  knob, and the tower-to-tower spread on identical labels (±1.6) is larger than
  the entire effect. One cell landing 0.58 high out of eleven tries is just the
  best of eleven draws.

  Three things did survive, and two are useful:

  1. The margin is the useful half; replay is harmful (79.27 / 77.15 / 74.35).
  Upweighted CE on a ~50%-mislabelled buffer is unbounded and keeps pushing on
  noise; the hinge saturates and stops.
  2. RER's recoverability filter made it worse. Restricting to the 305 failures
  a sibling tower already solves returns test to exactly baseline. The
  principled variant loses to the crude one — either the "irreducible" cases
  still supply useful gradient, or a 4-tower detector is too coarse.
  3. The recoverability curve — this is the real finding:

  ┌──────────────────────┬───────┬─────────────┐
  │ consensus confidence │ wrong │ recoverable │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────┤
  │ < 0.90               │ 247   │ 92–93%      │
  ├──────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────┤
  │ > 0.95               │ 425   │ 26%         │
  └──────────────────────┴───────┴─────────────┘

  The ultra-confident failures are 74% irreducible and the majority of all 
  failures. That quantifies D.11's "39 of 179 where no member is right" on
  training data, and retro-explains both the −4.34 collapse and why conf>0.95
  filtering underperformed. A large part of the remaining gap is annotation 
  noise, not modelling headroom.

  And the diagnostic you'd want, run properly: against the ensemble's 198
  errors, every candidate is net-negative — CER −17, baseline −23, factorized
  −33, and the best the campaign ever produced is the 8B at −9. Nothing produces
  corrections the consensus lacks.

  Standing result: 70.32 choice-free / 70.62 for the fixed 19-member structure.
  Matched deberta/roberta baselines still running to close the last
  interpretability gap.

  # The new idea I would actually bet on                                        
                                                                                
  ## **Annotation-Policy Separation (APS)**                                     
                                                                                
  This is the first idea I'd try that attacks a problem your experiments have   
  now exposed but haven't directly modeled:                                     
                                                                                
  > **Your training label is not necessarily the same thing as the underlying   
  sentiment.**                                                                  
                                                                                
  You have evidence that a large fraction of the model's “confident failures”   
  are not recoverable by another model. The ledger itself interprets a large    
  part of the residual as **annotation noise**, not missing model capacity.     
                                                                                
  So stop treating every gold label as equally trustworthy.                     
                                                                                
  ### But don't do ordinary label cleaning.                                     
                                                                                
  Cleanlab-style:                                                               
                                                                                
  ```text wrong label → remove/relabel                                          
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  is dangerous here because **the benchmark annotation is the thing you must    
  reproduce at test time**.                                                     
                                                                                
  Instead learn two latent signals:                                             
                                                                                
  ```text semantic sentiment                                                    
          ↓                                                                     
  POS / NEU / NEG                                                               
                                                                                
  annotation realization                                                        
          ↓                                                                     
  what this dataset tends to mark as POS/NEU/NEG                                
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  Then train the final classifier to predict the **benchmark label**, but use   
  the semantic head as a regularizer rather than as the target.                 
                                                                                
  ---                                                                           
                                                                                
  # Why this is different from everything you've tried                          
                                                                                
  Your current training is essentially:                                         
                                                                                
  [                                                                             
  x \rightarrow z \rightarrow y_{gold}                                          
  ]                                                                             
                                                                                
  with every (y_{gold}) treated as unquestionable.                              
                                                                                
  APS becomes:                                                                  
                                                                                
  [                                                                             
  x                                                                             
  \rightarrow                                                                   
  \begin{cases}                                                                 
  z_{semantic}\                                                                 
  z_{annotation}                                                                
  \end{cases}                                                                   
  \rightarrow y_{gold}                                                          
  ]                                                                             
                                                                                
  The semantic head learns broad polarity structure.                            
                                                                                
  The annotation head learns the **dataset-specific realization/noise           
  pattern**.                                                                    
                                                                                
  Then:                                                                         
                                                                                
  [                                                                             
  p(y)=p_{\text{annotation}}(y\mid z_{semantic},x)                              
  ]                                                                             
                                                                                
  The critical point is that examples that look like anomalous label noise      
  don't get used to distort the underlying representation as violently as       
  ordinary CE does.                                                             
                                                                                
  ---                                                                           
                                                                                
  # The TARKAN-specific version                                                 
                                                                                
  Keep everything:                                                              
                                                                                
  ```text                                                                       
  text                                                                          
  image                                                                         
  aspect anchors                                                                
  teacher relevance                                                             
  teacher KG filtering                                                          
  KAN                                                                           
  auxiliary ASC                                                                 
  student-only inference                                                        
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  Only change the **ASC training objective after KAN**.                         
                                                                                
  You already have:                                                             
                                                                                
  [                                                                             
  z_k = KAN(t_k,\tilde v_k,\tilde g_k)                                          
  ]                                                                             
                                                                                
  from the actual TARKAN algorithm.                                             
                                                                                
  Add:                                                                          
                                                                                
  ```text                                                                       
  z_k                                                                           
   │                                                                            
   ├── semantic polarity head                                                   
   │       POS / NEU / NEG                                                      
   │                                                                            
   └── annotation-policy head                                                   
           POS / NEU / NEG                                                      
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  Then:                                                                         
                                                                                
  [                                                                             
  L =                                                                           
  L_{tag}                                                                       
  +\lambda_{anc}L_{anc}                                                         
  +\lambda_{asc}L_{asc}                                                         
  +\lambda_{rel}L_{rel}                                                         
  +\lambda_{kg}L_{kg}                                                           
  +\lambda_s L_{semantic}                                                       
  +\lambda_a L_{annotation}                                                     
  ]                                                                             
                                                                                
  But the clever part is **how (L_{semantic}) is constructed**.                 
                                                                                
  ---                                                                           
                                                                                
  # The key trick: agreement-weighted semantics                                 
                                                                                
  Use OOF predictions from several independently trained models.                
                                                                                
  For each training aspect:                                                     
                                                                                
  ```text 4/4 models agree with gold                                            
      → high label confidence                                                   
                                                                                
  3/4                                                                           
      → medium                                                                  
                                                                                
  2/4                                                                           
      → uncertain                                                               
                                                                                
  0–1/4                                                                         
      → suspicious                                                              
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  But **do not replay the suspicious example**.                                 
                                                                                
  Instead, use agreement to decide how strongly its gold label should affect    
  the semantic representation:                                                  
                                                                                
  [                                                                             
  w_i = \text{agreement}(i)                                                     
  ]                                                                             
                                                                                
  So:                                                                           
                                                                                
  ```text                                                                       
  consensus + gold agree                                                        
          → strong semantic supervision                                         
                                                                                
  consensus disagrees with gold                                                 
          → weak semantic supervision                                           
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  The annotation head still gets the original benchmark label.                  
                                                                                
  This is very different from CER.                                              
                                                                                
  CER said:                                                                     
                                                                                
  > “model is wrong → push harder.”                                             
                                                                                
  APS says:                                                                     
                                                                                
  > **“model is wrong → perhaps don't distort the latent semantic               
  representation; let the annotation head absorb the irregularity.”**           
                                                                                
  That is directly motivated by your 74% ultra-confident failure/noise result.  
                                                                                
  ---                                                                           
                                                                                
  # There is an even better source of supervision: t2017                        
                                                                                
  Your latest protocol discovered that **t2017 is the only independent control  
  that has actually falsified a positive experiment**.                          
                                                                                
  So use it differently.                                                        
                                                                                
  **Do not pool t2017 labels into t2015.**                                      
                                                                                
  You already proved that changes the aspect-density prior and hurts.           
                                                                                
  Instead:                                                                      
                                                                                
  ### Train the semantic head on BOTH datasets.                                 
                                                                                
  ```text t2015:                                                                
  annotation head + semantic head                                               
                                                                                
  t2017:                                                                        
  semantic head ONLY                                                            
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  That gives you:                                                               
                                                                                
  ```text semantic representation                                               
            ↑                                                                   
      t2015 + t2017                                                             
                                                                                
  annotation realization                                                        
            ↑                                                                   
         t2015 only                                                             
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  This is extremely important.                                                  
                                                                                
  You're not transferring the t2017 **label prior** into the t2015 classifier.  
                                                                                
  You're transferring **general Twitter sentiment structure**.                  
                                                                                
  That attacks the exact problem the pooled-training experiment exposed:        
  t2017's different annotation density. You're deliberately preventing its      
  annotation policy from entering the t2015 decision head.                      
                                                                                
  This is a genuinely different hypothesis from your failed pooling experiment. 
                                                                                
  ---                                                                           
                                                                                
  # And it is cheap on T4                                                       
                                                                                
  You don't need another 7B.                                                    
                                                                                
  Your existing:                                                                
                                                                                
  ```text TARKAN BERTweet + CLIP + KAN                                          
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  remains.                                                                      
                                                                                
  You simply add one semantic ASC head.                                         
                                                                                
  For t2017:                                                                    
                                                                                
  ```text L_semantic                                                            
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  For t2015:                                                                    
                                                                                
  ```text L_semantic + L_annotation                                             
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  Then at inference on t2015:                                                   
                                                                                
  ```text semantic representation                                               
          ↓                                                                     
  annotation head                                                               
          ↓                                                                     
  POS / NEU / NEG                                                               
  ```                                                                           
                                                                                
  So the final output remains the benchmark's annotation convention.            
                                                                                
  ---                                                                           
                                                                                
  # Why I think this has more upside than CER                                   
                                                                                
  CER was asking:                                                               
                                                                                
  > “Can I force the model to memorize cases where the family is wrong?”        
                                                                                
  You just demonstrated that the answer is basically **no**, and the

  APS instead asks:

  decisions?”**                                                                 
                                                                                
  That's a fundamentally different failure mode.                                
                                                                                
  And your t2017 observation makes it testable.                                 
                                                                                
  ---

  ]                                                                             
                                                                                
  Then the annotation head can learn the weird cases.                           
                                                                                
  This avoids repeating the −0.97 factorization failure.
